Six transaction scopes are reported, each with error_count 0: "add product to cart" (437 samples; p50 3, p95 30, p99 72, max 78), "cart" (437; p50 9, p95 42, p99 49, max 187), "checkout" (437; p50 13, p95 45, p99 85, max 444), "home" (438; p50 27, p95 61, p99 96, max 904), "product" (437; p50 10, p95 46, p99 83, max 108), "reset cart" (437; p50 3, p95 7, p99 47, max 75). The overall max (904) equals the "home" max (904).

What the evidence does not contain: no latency or throughput policy_check, no capacity bound (LOWER_BOUND / UPPER_BOUND / BOUNDED), no stage-level or load-level results, no generator guard or resource series, no anomaly-test result or anomalies_tested count, no time series or timestamps, and no clock relationship information. Response-time behaviour and load-generator conditions are therefore reported but unevaluated, and no temporal ordering can be inferred.

The deterministic verdict (VALID / COMPLETE / PASS) is preserved unchanged; nothing below alters it. The advice is limited to bounded operator actions: inspect the JTL and policy configuration, configure additional policy rules if response times are in scope, verify clocks before any ordering claim, and rerun with a longer window or additional load levels if tail precision or capacity behaviour matters.

hypotheses.observation: The evidence contains a single policy_check, "overall-errors" (metric error_rate_ratio, observed 0/2623, operator lte, threshold 0.01, status PASS), and policy_verdict is PASS. No policy_check references latency_ms or throughput_rps, although the transaction summaries report latency maxima of 904 ms ("home") and 444 ms ("checkout") and p99 values from 47 ms to 96 ms.
hypotheses.possible_explanation: The policy set configured for this run may cover only overall error rate, so response-time and throughput numbers are surfaced as descriptive summaries without being judged. On that reading, PASS speaks to the error-rate rule only and carries no statement about latency; this is a coverage question about the policy set, not a defect in the run.
hypotheses.recommended_check: Inspect the policy configuration used for this run and list which metrics have rules and which do not. If response times are a product objective, add latency rules (for example per-transaction p95 or p99 thresholds) and re-evaluate; a missing rule is not a pass.

hypotheses.observation: Two transaction scopes show a large gap between their p95 and p99/max: "reset cart" reports p50 3 ms, p95 7 ms, p99 47 ms, max 75 ms over 437 samples; "add product to cart" reports p50 3 ms, p95 30 ms, p99 72 ms, max 78 ms over 437 samples.
hypotheses.possible_explanation: A very small subset of samples in the upper tail may be materially slower than the bulk, which can arise from first-iteration or cold-path costs, connection or cache warm-up, or intermittent contention. With 437 samples the p99 is determined by only a handful of the slowest records, so a few outliers can move it substantially. The evidence does not identify which of these applies.
hypotheses.recommended_check: Inspect the per-sample records for these two labels in the source JTL, ordered by timestamp, and check whether the slow samples cluster near the start of the window or are scattered; also record their response codes and the latency-versus-elapsed split. Treat any pattern found as a candidate explanation until confirmed by a rerun.

hypotheses.observation: The "home" scope is the only one with 438 samples (the other five have 437), and it carries the highest central and tail latencies of the six (p50 27 ms, p95 61 ms, p99 96 ms) plus the run maximum of 904 ms, which equals the overall max of 904 ms.
hypotheses.possible_explanation: "home" may be the first sampler of each iteration, which would be consistent with one extra execution relative to the other labels, and an early position in an iteration can coincide with cold caches or connection setup. The identical 904 ms maximum in the "home" and overall scopes is consistent with the same single sample being the largest in both scopes. Neither the extra sample nor the maximum is explained by the evidence.
hypotheses.recommended_check: Inspect the test plan and the JTL to confirm the intended iteration structure and sampler order, and locate the 904 ms "home" record by position in the window, response code, and elapsed-versus-latency fields. Confirm whether one extra "home" sample is expected rather than a duplicated or misattributed record.

hypotheses.observation: Every throughput_rps entry in the evidence shares the same denominator 44986, and sample counts are 2623 overall and 437–438 per transaction. The evidence presents a single overall scope plus six transaction scopes, with no stage, phase, or load-level breakdown.
hypotheses.possible_explanation: The analysis appears to describe one run window at one load level. Under that reading there is no second load point or phase split to compare against, so nothing in this evidence distinguishes steady-state behaviour from ramp-up or ramp-down effects, and tail percentiles rest on a small sample base.
hypotheses.recommended_check: Inspect the run configuration and the JTL time range to confirm the window length and whether ramp-up, steady state, and ramp-down are separable. If tail precision or load-dependent behaviour matters, rerun with a longer steady-state window and additional load levels so that comparisons stay within the same scope and window.
